sidecar.text:
The Richat Structure is situated
near Ouadane on the Adrar Plateau
within the Adrar Region of Mauritania.

Visible from space
as a massive desert landmark,

the concentric formation has served as a
visual reference point for space shuttle

crews. Its documented scale depends
on the observational method:

geological field surveys record
the feature at 40 kilometres across,

though satellite observations describe
it as spanning almost 50 kilometres.
What physical processes formed

this circular geological formation
in the Sahara? Geologists identify

the structure as an eroded dome created
when a subsurface igneous intrusion

deformed the overlying sedimentary
rock into concentric

rings. The structural characteristics
display distinct layering and magmatic

features. By one estimate, the sedimentary
rock layers that form the outer rings of

the structure dip outward
at angles between 10 and 20 degrees.

Framing the complex
are concentric gabbroic ring dikes,

consisting of an inner ring about 30
metres wide and an outer ring about 70
metres wide. At the core, by one estimate,

the heart of the structure features
a siliceous breccia covering an area

at least 30 kilometres in diameter,
reaching a thickness of at least 40 metres

at its center. The geological origins of
the Richat Structure were once a matter of

scientific debate. The feature was
initially considered an extraterrestrial

impact crater. However, the impact
theory was disproved when suspected

shock-metamorphism coesite was identified
in 1969 as mislabeled barite.

Subsequent geochemical analyses
established a terrestrial timeline:

dating of the carbonatite rocks shows they
cooled between 94 and 104 million years

ago, closely matching the hydrothermal
event that produced the central breccia.

Physical evidence across the terrain
establishes a prolonged record of human

presence. Prehistoric human habitation is
evidenced by exceptional accumulations of

Acheulean artifacts alongside
Middle Stone Age Aterian tools dating from
roughly 145,000 to 29,000 years ago.

Later mortuary traditions
also appear across the site;

by one estimate, thousands of prehistoric
stone burial mounds built in various

distinct architectural styles line
the protruding dikes of the formation.

While these material finds
document human activity,

the physical record also
refutes alternative speculation.

Fringe theories proposing the formation as
Plato's lost city of Atlantis are refuted

by geological reality,
as the feature is an ancient,

natural inland terrestrial dome
rather than a sunken island.

Through decades of field surveys
and geochemical analyses,

the Richat Structure has been established
as an eroded geological dome shaped by

deep-seated igneous processes
and prolonged erosion.

In October 2022, the International Union
of Geological Sciences recognized this

scientific value by designating the
formation as one of the world's first 100
official geological heritage sites.

With its origin grounded
in verified terrestrial processes,

what questions remain for field
researchers studying the formation and its
prehistoric human occupations?
